newsitem.title: UK: EMU positive for European corporate credit - S&P.
newsitem.headline: EMU positive for European corporate credit - S&P.

text.p: Standard & Poor's said the net effect of European and Monetary Union (EMU) should be broadly positive for credit trends within European companies, but is not likely to trigger substantial changes in corporate ratings.

"Greater competition fostered by a larger and deeper domestic market and greater price and cost transparency are likely to benefit successful and efficient companies," said Rupert Atkinson, director of Corporate Ratings, in a report.
S&P said as the universe of rated European corporates was skewed towards this type of company, the outlook was generally positive for corporate credit trends.
"A number of other factors are likely to have a beneficial impact on some corporates," S&P said in a statement.

"The cost of capital for corporates in some countries may be reduced if interest and inflation rates stabilise at lower than the weighted average of the participating countries, although interest rates may rise for countries at the heart of Europe," the agency said.
Borrowing should generally be easier in a larger and more liquid capital market and weaker credits should have easier access to the capital markets, it said.

"The most straightforward benefits of a single currency stem from the reduction in cross-border financial transaction costs within the EMU zone, via the elimination of foreign exchange risks and costs," said Atkinson.

Smaller companies, which were more likely to suffer from such costs, should reap the greatest benefits in this area. The disappearance of exchange rate risk might also encourage longer-term investment abroad, S&P said.
A number of costs and drawbacks offset the broadly positive factors associated with EMU, said the agency.

"It seems fairly clear that European economic growth rates will be impaired in the rush to meet public debt and budget deficit criteria stipulated in the Maastricht treaty; this is expected to have a short term negative impact on profitability," S&P said.

"More significantly, corporates will incur substantial one-off and transitional costs in switching to the euro, in information technology, accounting and financial management, tax, legal and payment systems, marketing and product planning."
S&P said the retailing sector was likely to be particularly badly affected.

"Another problem facing companies in countries that don't join EMU in the first wave is that they will incur many of the costs involved without initially reaping all of the benefits of the single currency," the agency said.
"At the general level, EMU's effects are likely to be broadly positive for rated corporates, though the impact will vary by sector and possibly by company size," said S&P.

The agency also considered the political context, and highlighted the risk of regional and national unemployment problems, given low job mobility and inflexible labor markets within Europe and the removal of exchange rate management as an economic tool.
